strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: selectively missing sensitive attributes can undermine fairness interventions that rely on independent imputation.
Jointly training an imputation adversary and a fairness adversary is an intuitive approach that accommodates partially observed sensitive information.

The evaluation covers six real datasets, synthetic graphs, GCN/GAT backbones, varying attribute availability, and scalability. Reported improvements are promising: on Bail, BFtS achieves 6.70% demographic-parity disparity versus FairGNN's 7.90%, with F1 improving from 0.84 to 0.85.
weaknesses: Theorem 2 is false as stated. Its proof equates maximizing Jensen–Shannon divergence between embedding distributions with maximizing demographic-parity disparity after prediction. A noninvertible prediction head does not preserve this maximization. For example, let h=(u,v) contain independent fair bits and predict v. Imputing either u or v achieves maximal embedding JS divergence, but the respective prediction disparities are 0 and 1. Thus the central worst-case imputation guarantee is invalid.

Theorems 2–3 analyze Eq. 7 after omitting the classification and imputation losses used in Eqs. 4 and 6. Consequently, they do not establish zero demographic-parity disparity for the actual regularized training objective. Minimizing fairness alone also admits trivial constant predictions. Moreover, the uncertainty set U is unspecified, and membership of the true sensitive assignment is not established; robustness against learned imputations therefore does not guarantee fairness for the true groups.

Other theoretical arguments contain fundamental errors. Theorem 1's reduction assigns every example y=1, making label-based demographic-parity disparity zero for every partition with two nonempty groups; this cannot encode minimum k-union. The convergence discussion also incorrectly states that disjoint-support distributions have JS divergence zero: their divergence is log(2). Constant imputations instead leave one group-conditional distribution undefined.

The experiments do not substantiate general adversarial robustness. Downstream comparisons primarily use the fixed degree-based missingness heuristic; random and targeted missingness are compared mainly through imputation correlations, without an adaptive attack against BFtS. Figure 2 also treats decreasing signed correlation as decreasing bias, although a sign reversal can preserve or increase absolute disparity.

The ablations do not adequately isolate the proposed mechanism. Although LDAM versus cross-entropy is evaluated, an otherwise identical beta=0 model and an independent LDAM imputer are missing. These controls are needed to distinguish adversarial coupling from improved imputation training. The completely missing setting compares only against RNF despite discussing several other methods that operate without demographics.

The method and evaluation protocol are insufficiently specified. Eq. 1 contains predictions instead of ground-truth labels and therefore expresses prediction entropy rather than supervised cross-entropy. The paper does not explain differentiation through the hard group assignments in Eq. 3. Validation/test splits, optimizer settings, learning rates, and training budgets are incompletely documented, while observed-attribute percentages refer to all nodes on page 18 but training nodes on page 27.
